author: Charlotte Brontë (Retold by Clare West)
introFa: کتاب «Jane Eyre» نوشته Charlotte Brontë (Retold by Clare West) یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Jane Eyre»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Brontë Studies, Vol. 30, March 2005 © The Brontë Society 2005 doi: 10.1179/147489304x18948 PAULA REGO’S JANE EYRE PRINTS: EXHIBITION AT THE BRONTË PARSONAGE MUSEUM 7 AUGUST–19 SEPTEMBER 2004 By Jane Sellars Paula Rego’s art is bold and beautiful, and it was a bold and beautiful step on the part of the Brontë Parsonage Museum to place an exhibition of Rego’s Jane Eyre prints throughout the Parsonage for the 2004 summer season. Prior to this exhibition, Rego’s Jane Eyre had been shown in quite a different but more conventional gallery setting at David Wright’s Artsmill, a converted mill space in Hebden Bridge (16 June to 25 July 2004). I was thrilled to be invited to open the Artsmill exhibition in June, and to hear Germaine Greer open the Haworth show on a balmy evening in August with a speech that rocked the rooks out of their graveyard roosts. Greer spoke with passion about the art of both Paula Rego and Charlotte Brontë. Another renowned scholar, Marina Warner, wrote a brilliant essay about the Rego Jane Eyre prints in the Tate Magazine (issue 8), in which she says of artist and writer that ‘as storytellers they are kith and kin’. It would seem to be a marriage made in heaven, and where better to show these images than at the Brontë Parsonage Museum? One must also not forget that art was a hugely important part of the Brontës’ lives. In fact, Charlotte had a serious, well-documented ambition to be an artist herself. Christine Alexander and I, working on our book the Art of the Brontës, discovered that Charlotte exhibited two of her own drawings at the Leeds Society for the Encouragement of the Fine Arts in 1832 when she was just sixteen. The show at the Parsonage consisted of fifteen lithographs, varying in scale and inten- sity of colour, from the small, monochromatic image ‘Inspection’, in which a miniature Jane Eyre is hoisted onto a high stool under the baleful glare of Mr Brocklehurst, to the vivid large-scale triptych, ‘Getting Ready for the Ball’. Daringly, Rego’s work was displayed throughout the house, starting with a series of prints mounted on easels in the Dining Room, and progressing on to Mr Brontë’s study, Mr Nicholls’ study, the children’s study and Mr Brontë’s bedroom. The display of contemporary art in an historic house setting is not a new idea, but it was a first for the Brontë Parsonage Museum, and for that it must be commended. However, there was an unevenness about the way the works were exhibited that, according to the visitors’ book, led to the art being perceived as an intrusion in the rooms. It was clear that the idea was to layer Rego’s prints as a kind of additional narrative strand to the Brontë story which viewers could take or leave as they wished. Sometimes this worked, sometimes it did not. 84 Jane Sellars Portrait with Grandchildren’ and the singular black loneliness of the figure of ‘Jane Eyre’ retreating from us into the darkness, vied with each other for space and attention. ‘Girl Reading at a Window’ (Figure 1), with the young Jane hiding behind the library curtains to escape into her book, worked much better by itself in Mr Brontë’s bookish room. The image reminds one how the author’s feeling for visual art is ever present in Jane Eyre, from this very opening scene when we find young Jane consoling herself with Thomas Bewick’s illustrations. The poignant image ‘Crying’, of Jane weeping into the curtains, found its place in the monastic chill of Mr Nicholls’ study. ‘Pleasing Mr Rochester’, with Adèle dancing before her guardian, also seemed to fit with the masculinity of Mr Brontë’s bedroom, surrounded by Branwell’s portraits of local male worthies. But creative opportunities to enhance both art and setting were missed; sometimes very narrowly, as with the odd positioning of the powerful ‘Come To Me’ (Figure 2) on the stairway wall, a perfect location for the work, but not hung in precisely the right place. One began to yearn for the art curator’s eye. One of the most symbolic passages in Charlotte Brontë’s novel occurs when Jane Eyre draws her self portrait, using rough black chalks, and labels it fiercely ‘Portrait of a Governess, disconnected, poor, and plain’. For me, this Rego image Figure 1. ‘Girl reading at window’ Downloaded by [University Library Utrecht] at 17:39 16 March 2016

85 Paula Rego’s JANE EYRE Prints of Jane Eyre, her body clenched in emotional pain, is at one with Charlotte’s literary invention. Pictures need space, and pictures of the power of Rego’s Jane Eyre need more space than most. This was especially evident in the way that ‘Refectory’, ‘Inspection’, and ‘Jane and Helen’, all scenes from Lowood School, were jammed together on a too short stretch of wall in the exhibition room. Whatever the few shortcomings of the actual display and interpretation of Rego’s work in the Parsonage, one was still struck by how passionately and vividly Rego’s visual imaginings bond with Charlotte Brontë’s marvellous story. For me, and I think for many other viewers, Paula Rego has achieved something quite remarkable with her Jane Eyre series. She has taken the power of the text and transformed it into its absolute visual equivalent. The way she has used, for example, distortions of scale and extremes of dark and light to parallel the psychological drama of the novel is compelling. In the end, I came away from the Parsonage with the sense that it was both wonderful and inspiring to see Rego’s Jane Eyre prints in the house that nurtured the creative genius of Charlotte Brontë and her extraordinary siblings. Above all, I was reminded that this was a place of remarkable creativity. She was previously Director of the Brontë Parsonage Museum and Curator at Harewood House. She is the co-author with Christine Alexander of the Art of the Brontës, and author of Charlotte Brontë published by the British Library.
